title: Prompt Engineering 101: five research-backed rules for asking AI better questions
summary: Ruben Hassid summarizes recent academic papers on prompting modern LLMs. Key lessons: keep questions neutral, drop "step by step", verify every AI-cited source, limit prompts to about 3 rules, and give a clear goal instead of examples. The final "One Prompt" template is paywalled.

principles.text: Keep prompts neutral: avoid tag questions and yes/no framing that bias the AI toward agreeing with you.
principles.quote: Just like when you ask a friend, don’t make them answer the way you want them to answer. Keep it neutral. Avoid yes/no questions.

principles.text: Skip "step by step" instructions; a short role ("as a reliability engineer") added to your question beat chain-of-thought.
principles.quote: The most famous “Let’s think step by step” LOST to asking normally.

principles.text: Never trust AI-cited sources on confidence; open and verify every link, since even expert reviewers miss hallucinated citations.
principles.quote: If professional reviewers can’t catch AI-hallucinated papers, you won’t either. You must open every link:

principles.text: Limit a single prompt to about 3 rules; split extra requirements into a second pass that checks them one at a time.
principles.quote: 12 of the 15 models can’t reliably hold more than 3 rules.

principles.text: State a clear goal and context rather than pasting examples, which can hurt modern models; let the AI ask for missing data.
principles.quote: Specifying a goal is the ultimate key to a good prompt.

principles.text: Prompt advice expires quickly as models change, so re-check techniques against recent research instead of trusting old tips.
principles.quote: AI changes so fast that techniques from before don’t work anymore.
